turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for fitting me in. Um, so, the main reason I’m here is... well, I'm a registered nurse, and things at work have just gotten to a point where I’m genuinely terrified I'm going to mess something up, because I just lose my train of thought constantly on the floor. And I mean *constantly*. 

The floor is always chaotic, obviously, but it’s like my brain has absolutely zero filter for any of it. I’ll be right in the middle of figuring out a really complex patient flow issue—you know, trying to mentally map out who is being discharged, who needs transport, where the new admissions are going, which takes a lot of mental juggling—and then an IV pump will beep. Not even my patient's pump, just a random pump down the hall. Or someone at the nurses' station will just ask another nurse a totally unrelated question about supplies, or a call light goes off three doors down. 

And just like that, the thought is completely gone. I'll just be standing there, and I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was even working on. It just vanishes into thin air. And in nursing, you really can't afford to just blank out like that, because everything is so time-sensitive and critical. So I end up standing there feeling like an absolute idiot, trying to retrace my mental steps, which takes forever. And then by the time I finally figure out what I was doing, something else beeps, or someone else talks, and the whole thing happens all over again. It’s just exhausting, honestly, trying to hold onto a single thought for more than ten seconds when there's so much going on around me, and I just feel like I'm constantly paddling against the current just to do the basic parts of my job, which I went to grad school for, so I should be able to handle this, but...

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being constantly distracted by extraneous stimuli at work, such as IV pumps, background conversations, and call lights, which causes them to lose their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with concentration and distractibility? Has this always been something you've struggled with, or is this something that's gotten much worse recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s... I mean, I think it’s definitely gotten significantly worse. Like, exponentially worse. It really became this massive, unavoidable problem almost exactly two years ago. That was when I stepped up and took on these expanded charge-nurse responsibilities on the unit. 

Before that, when I was just a regular staff nurse managing my own specific patient assignment, I could kind of... I don't know, I could build a little bubble around myself? I had my own clipboard, my own strict little routine, and I could just focus on my four or five patients and get through the shift. But when you're charge, you don't get a bubble. You are the point person for literally everything. The doctors rounding, the pharmacy calling about missing meds, the nursing assistants needing help with a lift, family members complaining at the front desk... it all funnels directly to you. 

So for the last two years, since I took on that expanded role, it's just been this escalating nightmare. Because suddenly I have to hold the entire floor's status in my head, and I just can't do it with all the noise. I mean, maybe looking back, I've always had to work a little harder than other people to keep my thoughts organized—like in grad school, I basically had to live in the absolute quietest corner of the library with foam earplugs just to get through my reading assignments—but it never felt dangerous, you know? It never felt like this. It’s really been these last two years with these new charge responsibilities where the distractibility has just completely taken over and made me feel like I'm losing my grip on a daily basis.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient notes having always had to work harder than others to keep their thoughts organized.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states that distractibility has completely taken over and that they cannot function with all the noise.

turns.doctor_question: When you were in elementary school or high school, did teachers ever mention that you had trouble paying attention in class, or did you struggle to sit still and focus on schoolwork back then?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes. I mean, honestly, yes. I guess when you put it like that, it’s always been there in some form, even if it wasn't a life-or-death nursing situation. Like, I distinctly remember my elementary school report cards—my mom actually kept a bunch of them in this big plastic tub in the attic, and I looked through them a few years ago when we were helping her move. And it was almost comical, because every single teacher, year after year, wrote almost the exact same thing in the comments section. They’d say, you know, "She’s a very bright girl, she has so much potential," but then the next sentence was always, always about how careless I was. 

"Careless" was the word they loved to use. Because I was constantly losing my worksheets. Like, literally losing them between the teacher handing them out at the front of the row and the paper making its way back to my desk. Or I’d actually manage to do the homework—which was a whole other ordeal—but then I’d just completely forget to turn it in. It would just sit in my backpack, crumpled at the bottom under my gym clothes, for weeks. 

And the only reason I even got through those early years was because my mom basically made it her second job to manage my brain. She would sit with me at the kitchen table every single night, right after dinner, and she’d have to physically sit there and keep redirecting me. Because if she got up to answer the phone or check on the laundry, I’d be staring out the window, or peeling the paper off my crayons, or just completely zoned out. She had to constantly tap the table and say, "Focus, look at the math problem, keep going." So yeah, I didn't struggle to sit still—I wasn't bouncing off the walls or anything—but focusing? Keeping track of things? That was a massive, massive struggle, even back then. I just kind of thought I’d outgrown it, or learned to manage it, until I became charge nurse and the wheels completely fell off.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a 'massive struggle' with focusing and zoning out unless her mother constantly redirected her.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient states she was 'constantly losing my worksheets' before they even made it to her desk.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes she would easily get distracted by staring out the window or peeling paper off crayons.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies struggling to sit still.
